Memorandum of Conversation, by the Acting Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs (Jernegan)

div.head:
No. 935
Memorandum of Conversation, by the Acting Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs (Jernegan)
div.p: Secret

list.item: United States Policy Toward Arab-Israeli Relations
Mr. Reuven Shiloah, Minister, Embassy of Israel
Acting Assistant Secretary John D. Jernegan

div.p: Ambassador Eban began by referring to his previous conversations with the Secretary last Summer and Fall and said he had called this time to offer “reflections on familiar themes”. These themes were (a) the security of Israel and (b) peace in the Middle East.

Since his last meeting with the Secretary in October, the Ambassador said there had been developments which were both encouraging and discouraging. On the negative side, Israel had noted no concrete steps to change the adverse situation created by America’s policy of arming the Arabs and by the Anglo-Egyptian base agreement.

Furthermore, Israel had noted a speech by the Syrian Prime Minister once again threatening Israel’s extinction. Other discouraging developments included a recent turbulent period on the Israeli-Egyptian frontier, the seizure by the Egyptians of the Bat Galim, the Alexandria trial of Jews charged with espionage and a development of Arab League thinking looking toward a defense organization linked with the West but excluding Israel.

On the encouraging side, the Ambassador said Israel notes evidence that the Western Powers have a better realization of the reality of the threat to Israel’s security. Many members of both parties of the British House of Commons had recently expressed their sympathetic understanding of Israel’s exposed position. In the same debate Foreign Secretary Eden had made a very encouraging statement regarding the action Britain would take if necessary under the Tripartite Declaration of 1950 and Britain’s policy of maintaining a military balance between Israel and the Arab States collectively. It was true that Mr. Eden’s statement did not constitute a contractual obligation, but since he had made it publicly, Israel hoped he would be able to make it directly to the Government of Israel as well. Knowing the close cooperation among Britain, France and the United States on this subject, Israel hoped that all three countries could make similar official statements. There were other indications of the realization in several countries that Israel has a case in this security question. The Ambassador had had a conversation with the French Prime Minister who had shown his realization that the problem is real. A recent speech by the Solicitor General of the United States had likewise been encouraging. He had made four points:
1. That the Secretary of State was evaluating our policy in the Middle East;
2. That we understood Israel’s feeling of insecurity;
3. That we thought we could take measures to allay these feelings; and
4. We hoped Israel would cooperate to this end.

This statement had had a calming effect in Israel by showing that the problem was not being ignored. At the same time, it had increased the expectancy of the people of Israel that something would be done.
The Ambassador interjected that some American newspapers attributed this increased awareness of Israel’s problem to “non international factors”. This was wrong.

In the Ambassador’s view there were three immediate needs: First, to arrange a security guarantee to Israel; second, to maintain a balance of military strength between Israel and the Arab States; and third, to include Israel in any defense arrangements in the
area. He thought we might be approaching the time when these needs could be resolved and Israel’s security could cease to be the main subject of discussions between us.

He hoped that the resolution of this security question could be handled separately and eliminated before we went on to deal with the broader question of Arab-Israel relations. Israel had been pleased to note the great emphasis being placed in American statements on “peace” as a major objective of the United States in the Middle East. Israel would welcome any constructive and prudent initiative to solve some of the outstanding problems between herself and the Arabs. In this connection, the Israel Government had been interested in the recent visit of Mr. Shuckburgh and in his thinking on area matters. However, he had not said very much that was new or hopeful. The Ambassador feared that unless Britain and the United States had some further thoughts on the subject, we might get onto the wrong track. If we (presumably Britain and the United States) were to make suggestions calling for unilateral sacrifices by Israel, if Israel had to give up any of her extremely limited territory or repatriate refugees (thus creating an internal security problem), this would not lead to a solution but merely to a “running fight” between Israel and the United Kingdom and the United States, and to the maintenance of the status quo. The Ambassador hoped we would not adopt such a line.

Mr. Eban added that Israel did not wish to seem negative and thought she could be helpful in working toward a solution. Recently Mr. Eden had asked the Israeli Ambassador in London for suggestions. Ambassador Elath had been instructed to reply that Israel could offer a free port at Haifa for Jordan in return for a relaxation of the Arab boycott. This could be done even ahead of a general settlement. He had also suggested that Israel might arrange to pay compensation for lost refugee property in return for a lifting of the Egyptian blockade in the Suez Canal. (The blockade itself, by increasing Israel’s financial costs contributed substantially to Israel’s inability at present to pay compensation.) These were merely illustrations, Ambassador Eban said, and he was not authorized to make any proposals but settlement on the points he had mentioned would have great effect. He suggested that we tackle items of this kind rather than the extremely emotional territorial question.

In the meantime, the Ambassador went on, it was important to keep Arab-Israel relations from getting worse, especially in the case of Egypt. The Alexandria trial and the Bat Galim case held serious dangers. The Ambassador observed that he knew of the efforts we were making. He left the implication that we should do even more. He made the further remark that several maritime nations
had indicated to Israel that they considered the Bat Galim case as of direct concern to them because it involved the right of freedom of navigation of international waterways.
The Acting Secretary thanked Ambassador Eban for his observations and proceeded to comment as follows, reading carefully from notes prepared by NEA for this purpose:

The Secretary’s personal review of the Arab-Israel situation goes forward. It is to the interest of all concerned that these studies be pursued with due deliberation. He did not wish at this juncture to comment on Sir Anthony Eden’s remarks. We are pleased to note that the situation as regards public opinion in Israel now appears somewhat calmer.
We have consistently held to the position that any military assistance which we may grant to the Near East states must be delivered under conditions whereby the security of Israel is not threatened.

We are continuing our efforts to persuade Egypt to conform with the SC resolution regarding the right of transit of the Suez Canal for all ships of all flags. We feel that there is a good chance of ultimately obtaining what Israel and other maritime states desire if we can have a quiet atmosphere to negotiate the gradual relaxation of the Egyptian restrictions. Israel should not crowd the issue and put Egypt publicly “on the spot”.

We maintain our serious concern over the situation along Israel borders. We have in the past spoken to Egypt on this matter, not without some effect. We are prepared to do so again if we feel that the situation warrants such action.

Our Ambassador in Cairo has informally indicated to the Egyptian Government that Egypt’s handing down death sentences to the accused eleven Jews could seriously affect the security situation in the area.

The Ambassador agreed that public opinion in Israel is now calmer. He attributed this partly to increased Israeli confidence in the UNTSO under the “statesman-like leadership” of General Burns, partly to the success of Ambassador Lawson in getting across the broader aspects of American-Israeli relations and partly to recent American statements such as that of the Solicitor General and the assurance that Israeli’s problems had the personal attention of the Secretary of State.

He also agreed that the frontiers are more tranquil at this moment and said he did not suggest any new efforts by the United States in Egypt in this regard. He emphasized that an important element in the improvement on the frontiers is Israel’s own contribution through a very purposeful policy of non-retaliation. Israel had shown restraint despite continued Arab provocations. Under
the previous Israel security policy, these Arab provocations would have produced reprisals. The present policy of restraint is that of Prime Minister Sharett. There are elements in Israel which favor a more militant attitude. Ambassador Eban hoped the West would so act as to give support to the moderates.

The Ambassador concluded the substantive part of the conversation by referring to two instances in which Arab intransigence not merely blocked good relations between Israel and the Arab States themselves but also between Israel and third countries. One of these involved Israel’s desire to save money by buying Iranian oil. Her relations with Iran, although not fully normal, were friendly and Israel could buy oil from that country. The difficulty was that Egypt probably would prevent its passage through the Suez Canal. The second instance involved a sale of twenty spitfire aircraft by Israel to Burma. The sale had been completed and the aircraft transferred to the Burmese flag. They were to have been flown to Burma by a British firm but those which had begun the journey had been held up in Beirut and Baghdad simply because they had originally come from Israel. This showed the extent to which the Arabs carried their boycott.
The Acting Secretary assured the Ambassador that he would report to the Secretary on their conversation as soon as Mr. Dulles returned.
